essential: Tommy climbs the filthy stairs. He reasons that 'Mr. Brown' is a password, and that entering the meeting room would be a colossal risk because more identification may be required.
He hides in the recess behind the torn velvet curtain, opposite the meeting-room door and overlooking the stairs, and watches through its slits.

Arrivals use the signal knock and are asked their number. Keep the bearded, precise-voiced German chairman's 'Your number, comrade?' and the brutal reply 'Fourteen, gov'nor' / 'Correct'. Tommy is glad he did not enter.

The other arrivals: an Irish Sinn Feiner; a quiet, shabby, clerk-like man; a working man with a vaguely familiar face; and a commanding, well-dressed man whose face Tommy half-knows but cannot name. Include Tommy's wonder at who holds this varied chain.

The pale Slavonic last arrival seems to see through the curtain. All rise for him. Mr. Brown 'cannot be present'; the guest suggests Brown may be among them, and the men eye each other in fear. He is seated at the head as 'Number One', and Number Fourteen shuts the door.
Tommy removes his shoes and tries the handle with great care; the door is bolted inside. He restores the handle and his tenacity persists.
He enters the empty next-door bedroom, draws the rusty bolt on the communicating door, and hears the meeting but cannot see past the portière. He identifies speakers by voice only.

Irish business: money for a 'reign of terror' in Ireland; money routed via Irish Americans and 'Mr. Potter', with the American voice's caveat; the difficulty of landing ammunition; and the commanding man's 'Think of the feelings of Belfast'. Mention the newspaper loan and the denial from Moscow briefly.
The German reports 'by--Mr. Brown' on the unions. The date is the 29th. The Labour leaders must think the strike is their own show. Keep Number One on honest men.
'Clymes must go', assigned to Number Fourteen. Keep the gloves with a housebreaker's fingerprints and Fourteen's relish for blood running in the streets.

The German doubts the Labour leaders will strike. The document would assure success, but they do not have it. Only 'a girl' may know where it is; 'This case is different'. Tommy is struck down mid-answer and the striker is not named.

title: THE ADVENTURES OF TOMMY
voice_profile: Brisk, light third-person narration that stays close to Tuppence or Tommy and slips into their idiom ('keep her end up', 'old bean', 'If that isn't a Hun, I'm a Dutchman!'). Comedy and danger sit side by side. Short dialogue exchanges carry most of the action. Wry authorial asides deflate the drama ('a reversion that aroused in Tuppence a faint misgiving'). The narration reports the characters' own reasoning step by step, such as Tuppence 'intoxicated with the success of truthfulness' or Tommy weighing the risks 'in his usual slow and steady way'. Villains speak in heightened melodramatic idiom, which is set against the young heroes' slangy understatement.
book_context: A 1920s thriller in alternating Tuppence and Tommy strands. Its central device is the unseen 'Mr. Brown', who hides as a nondescript background figure and whose name is used openly. Small details are planted and later paid off: the clerk called Brown and the telephone message with no telephone; the name Rita, which leads to Mrs. Vandemeyer; the false Jane Finn at a Paris pensionnat; Number 14; the recess and curtain in the Soho house; the date of the 29th; the half-recognised faces of the conspirators; the girl who cannot be made to speak. Chapter II begins Tuppence's bluffing streak and her open love of money. Chapter VIII starts Tommy's captivity and lays out the conspiracy's stakes. Neither chapter may reveal who Mr. Brown is, who Number One is, or that Jane has lost her memory.
